title: NASA's Swift observatory to burn up on re-entry around November 2 after 22 years in orbit
excerpt: NASA's Swift observatory, built for two years and worked for 22, is expected to re-enter Earth's atmosphere around November 2 after a failed rescue boost.
content:
NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory — a spacecraft built for a two-year mission that kept working for more than two decades — is expected to plunge into Earth's atmosphere around November 2, ending one of the most productive runs in space astronomy. Most of the observatory will burn up; researchers expect a small amount of debris to fall into the ocean.

Swift spent almost 22 years in orbit, slowly losing altitude until it could no longer hold its pointing steady. In July, a spacecraft launched on a fast-turnaround mission to boost Swift out of danger, but the rescue mission began to spin uncontrollably before reaching its target. Swift drifted so low — below 171 miles (275 kilometers) by October 20 — that it could not lock onto its astronomical targets, and NASA shut off science operations ahead of the spacecraft's fall. NASA formally announced the end of Swift science operations on October 23.

The loss is being felt across astronomy. Swift observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts — the most powerful explosions in the universe — along with black holes, the remnants of stellar explosions, active supermassive black holes in distant galaxies and comets in our own solar system, feeding roughly 7,000 scientific papers. "We're all definitely very sad. There's definitely grief," Caryl Gronwall, Swift's science operations team lead at Penn State, told Nature, which called the end of operations "dramatic and tragic."

Swift's story is also a case study in how long a well-built observatory can outlast its design life — and how solar activity can end it. Recent solar activity increased atmospheric drag on the spacecraft, accelerating its descent; a servicing mission that ended in August without a boost attempt, followed by a return to observations that increased drag further, left Swift sinking too fast to recover.

What to watch next: NASA's updated re-entry prediction as November 2 approaches, and where any surviving debris is tracked to fall. Swift's archive — two decades of burst and transient observations — remains available for scientists to explore.
